section.title: Witness Against Israel
section.sectionRationale: The first of the sermons of judgment. Amos defends his right to prophesy with a chain of cause-and-effect questions: nothing happens without a reason, and God does nothing without warning His prophets. Then he summons Israel's pagan enemies as witnesses to her oppression, and announces the tearing down of Bethel's altars and the mansions of the rich.
section.thesis: Election is not exemption but greater accountability; the God who reveals His purposes through His prophets has roared, and the judgment now falling on Israel's altars and ivory houses is neither random nor unannounced.
section.frameNote: Four movements: privilege that means greater accountability; the chain of inevitable cause and effect; foreign witnesses summoned against Israel; and the sentence on Bethel's altars and the great houses.

verses.text: Hear this word that the LORD has spoken against you, O children of Israel, against the whole family that I brought up out of the land of Egypt:
“Only you have I {{yada|known}} from all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.”

units.label: Cause and effect
units.note: the lion has roared, who will not fear

verses.text: Can two walk together without agreeing where to go?
Does a lion roar in the forest when he has no prey? Does a young lion growl in his den if he has caught nothing?
Does a bird land in a snare where no bait has been set? Does a trap spring from the ground when it has nothing to catch?
If a ram’s horn sounds in a city, do the people not tremble? If calamity comes to a city, has not the LORD caused it?
Surely the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets.
The lion has {{shaag|roared}}, who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken, who will not prophesy?
Proclaim to the citadels of Ashdod and to the citadels of Egypt: “Assemble on the mountains of Samaria; see the great unrest in the city and the acts of oppression in her midst.”
“For they know not how to do right,” declares the LORD. “They store up violence and destruction in their citadels.”
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: “An enemy will surround the land; he will pull down your strongholds and plunder your citadels.”

This is what the LORD says: “As the shepherd snatches from the mouth of the lion two legs or a piece of an ear, so the Israelites dwelling in Samaria will be rescued having just the corner of a bed or the cushion of a couch.

units.label: Bethel and the ivory houses fall
units.note: the horns of the altar cut off

verses.text: Hear and testify against the house of Jacob, declares the Lord GOD, the God of Hosts.
On the day I punish Israel for their transgressions, I will visit destruction on the altars of Bethel; the horns of the altar will be cut off, and they will fall to the ground.
I will tear down the winter house along with the summer house; the houses of ivory will also perish, and the great houses will come to an end,” declares the LORD.

yada.gloss: To know, but with far more than intellectual knowledge; it can mean to choose, to enter into intimate covenant relationship with. When God says only you have I known of all the families of the earth, He means Israel alone was set in covenant love. The shocking logic follows: such intimacy means greater, not lesser, accountability.

shaag.gloss: To roar, the sound of a lion over its prey. The shepherd Amos uses it to explain his own boldness: when the lion roars, fear is the only sane response, and when the Lord GOD speaks, prophesying is unavoidable. The roar that opened the book, Amos 1:2, now becomes the reason the prophet cannot keep silent.

basic.context: Amos begins the sermons of judgment by defending why he must speak. He reasons like a shepherd: effects have causes. A lion roars because it has prey; a trap springs because something touched it. So when disaster comes on a city, God is behind it, and He always warns His prophets first. Then Amos calls even Israel's pagan enemies to look at the oppression in Samaria, and announces that the altars of Bethel and the luxury houses of the rich will be torn down.
basic.hermeneutics: The key idea is that being chosen makes Israel more accountable, not less. God's special relationship with them is a reason for judgment when they rebel, not an excuse. The chain of questions defends the prophetic word: Amos speaks because God has spoken; the roar leaves him no choice.
basic.originalLanguages: God says only you have I known, yada, a word for intimate covenant choosing, and draws the surprising conclusion: therefore I will punish you. Amos explains his boldness with the lion's roar, shaag: when the lion roars you fear, and when the Lord GOD speaks you prophesy. The prophet cannot stay silent.
basic.typology: The prophet who must speak because God has spoken foreshadows Christ, the final Prophet and Word made flesh, and the whole line of witnesses God raises to call His people back. The horns of the altar cut off point to the futility of false worship and the need for the true altar and sacrifice.
basic.christ: Amos does nothing except relay what God reveals, pointing to Jesus, the Prophet who speaks only what the Father gives Him, and the Word Himself. The altars of Bethel, symbols of a corrupt, self-made religion, are torn down, clearing the way for the one true sacrifice offered by Christ, whose blood, unlike the horns of Bethel's altar, truly saves.
basic.god: God chooses in love but never winks at sin; intimacy with Him raises the standard. He is sovereign over history, behind even the calamities that fall on cities, yet He never acts without warning through His servants. And He is so committed to justice that He calls pagan nations to witness against His own people.
basic.crossReferences: Amos 3:7 is echoed wherever God reveals His plans to prophets. Luke 12:48 teaches that to whom much is given, much is required. Hebrews 1 shows God's final word spoken in His Son.
basic.oneStory: God's roar through Amos belongs to the long story of a God who warns before He judges and speaks before He acts, a story that climaxes when the Word Himself comes, and false altars give way to the one true sacrifice.

context.literary:
Chapter 3 begins a new kind of speech. The first two chapters were a sequence of oracles built on one formula. From here to the end of chapter 6 the book is organised around the call 'Hear this word,' which opens chapters 3, 4 and 5, 3:1, 4:1 and 5:1, and is followed by the cry 'Woe' in 5:18 and 6:1. In each case the prophet addresses the hearers directly and spells out the case against them.

Within chapter 3 the movement is in four parts. Verses 1 and 2 are a short, shocking thesis. Verses 3 to 8 are a chain of questions that grow in force: two people walking, a lion, a young lion, a bird, a trap, a ram's horn, a city struck by calamity. Verse 7 steps out of the series with a statement, and verse 8 closes it with a pair of questions that turn the argument back on the prophet. Verses 9 to 12 summon witnesses and give a verdict, and verses 13 to 15 end with a sentence that falls on the altar at Bethel and on the houses of the rich.

The questions have a structure of their own. The first one, 'Can two walk together without agreeing where to go?' is the most open. The next four are pairs that all move from effect to cause. A lion roars only if he has prey, a trap springs only if something has been caught. The fifth and sixth turn on the sound of a ram's horn and the arrival of calamity, and by that point the questions have moved from nature to history: there is a human warning and a divine cause. Each question expects the answer 'no.' By the time Amos reaches verse 8, the audience has said 'no' six times and is in no position to say 'no' to the seventh, which is whether a prophet can be silent when God has spoken.

The chapter is also bound together by a repeated verb. In verse 2 God says He will 'punish' Israel for its iniquities, and in verse 14 He says that on the day He 'punishes' Israel's transgressions He will 'visit' destruction on the altars of Bethel. The same word of visitation opens the chapter and closes it, and the thing that began as the privilege of being known ends as the visit of a Judge.
context.historical:
The 'whole family' of verse 1 is a larger group than the northern kingdom, since Amos defines it by the exodus, 'the whole family that I brought up out of the land of Egypt.' He is speaking in the north, but the words reach everyone who traced their descent to the exodus, Judah included. The note of election in verse 2 recalls the language of Deuteronomy 7:6-8, where God chose Israel not for size but out of love and oath. Hosea, a contemporary in the north, uses the same verb of God's care in the wilderness, Hosea 13:5.

The setting of the rest of the chapter is Samaria, the capital built by Omri and enlarged by Ahab, 1 Kings 16:24. It sat on a hill with higher ground around it, which is why Amos can summon witnesses to 'assemble on the mountains of Samaria,' verse 9, and look down into the city. The 'houses of ivory' recall Ahab's ivory palace, 1 Kings 22:39, and Amos speaks again of beds of ivory in 6:4. Ivory carvings have been recovered from the site of ancient Samaria, which fits the picture of a city of wealth. The winter and summer houses were the luxury of the very rich, who could afford separate homes for the seasons.

Bethel was the royal sanctuary set up by Jeroboam I with its golden calf, 1 Kings 12:28-33, and in the time of Amos it was the 'sanctuary of the king,' Amos 7:13. The horns of the altar were its four corner projections, where blood was applied and where fugitives might grasp hold and claim sanctuary, as Adonijah did in 1 Kings 1:50-51. To say that the horns will be cut off is therefore to say that there will be no refuge at the altar. The image of the shepherd who rescues scraps from the lion's mouth is also from the world Amos knew, where the law released a shepherd from liability if he brought back the torn remains as evidence, Exodus 22:13.
context.canonical:
The statement of verse 2 is among the most quoted principles in the Bible about privilege and responsibility. Moses had spoken of a people who were holy and chosen, Deuteronomy 7:6, and also warned that curses would follow unfaithfulness, Deuteronomy 28. Amos draws the logical consequence without softening it. The New Testament retains the idea. Jesus says, 'From everyone who has been given much, much will be required,' Luke 12:48, and Peter says that judgment begins with the family of God, 1 Peter 4:17. Paul, writing to the Romans, sets the advantage of Israel against its responsibility: they were entrusted with the words of God, Romans 3:1-2, and yet those who boast in the law dishonour God by breaking it, Romans 2:17-24.

The statement of verse 7, that the Lord God does nothing without revealing His plan to His prophets, has a long background. God asked of Abraham, 'Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?' Genesis 18:17, and Jeremiah complains of false prophets who have not 'stood in the council of the LORD to see and hear His word,' Jeremiah 23:18. It is taken up in the last book of the Bible, where the mystery of God is to be fulfilled 'just as He proclaimed to His servants the prophets,' Revelation 10:7. John 15:15 gives it a fresh turn by saying that Jesus has called His followers friends rather than servants, because He has made known to them everything He learned from the Father.

Verse 8 sets the compulsion of the prophet beside the fear of the hearer. Jeremiah describes the same inner fire, 'His message becomes a fire burning in my heart,' Jeremiah 20:9, and Paul writes, 'Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel,' 1 Corinthians 9:16. The altar horns of verse 14 appear in the story of Adonijah and Joab, 1 Kings 1:50-51 and 1 Kings 2:28, as the last place of shelter, and Hebrews 13:10 speaks of Christians as having 'an altar' of their own.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Amos had to answer a question that must have been asked in Samaria: by what right does a Judean shepherd say these things about us? Verses 3 to 8 are his reply. He did not volunteer for this. He compares his position to that of someone who hears a lion roar. The roar is not an invitation to debate; it is a fact that produces fear, and the fear produces action. When God has spoken, the one who hears has no real option about whether to repeat it. The point of the argument is that the authority of the word lies in its source and not in the prophet.

Amos also meant to answer a second question, the one the people really wanted to ask: how can this be, when we are God's people? The second verse is his answer, and it is meant to shock. Israel believed that being chosen made them safe. Amos tells them that being chosen has made them known, and what is known is accountable. The same fact on which they based their comfort becomes the ground of the charge.

His third aim is to bring the hearer into the courtroom. By summoning Ashdod and Egypt to look at Samaria, he reverses the usual picture of Israel as the witness against the pagans. The nations are now to observe Israel and conclude that what is going on there is worse than what goes on among them. And the closing verses ensure that nobody leaves thinking that this is only talk: the altar will fall and the ivory houses with it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes an exchange between God, His prophet and a people, and it describes the grounds on which God will judge. It does not offer a general rule that every disaster is a message about the sins of the victims. Verse 6 is sometimes read that way, with disastrous results for the sufferer. Jesus warns against exactly that inference when asked about those killed when the tower in Siloam fell, Luke 13:1-5. Amos is declaring that God stands behind the specific disasters of Israel's own covenant history, which He had warned about in the law, Deuteronomy 28. That is a different thing from reading every flood or accident as a verdict.

What does carry forward is the shape of the argument. Those who have been given much are responsible for much, so the church, which has the whole Bible and the Spirit of Christ, is asked to hold itself to a higher standard and not a lower one. It also carries forward the idea that God's word does not return empty and that those who speak it are bound to speak even when it costs them. Finally, the passage warns believers against reading God's favour as insurance. The people who most surely belong to God are those who most take His words seriously, and the answer to being known by Him is obedience, not complacency.

debates.question: What does it mean that the LORD has 'caused' calamity in a city, verse 6?

views.label: God sends disaster as judgment
views.case: The word for calamity, ra'ah, is the ordinary word for harm or disaster, and the verse says the LORD has 'done' it. Isaiah 45:7 says that He creates calamity, and Lamentations 3:37-38 asks whether good and adversity do not both come from the Most High. On this reading Amos is stating plainly that the disasters that fell on Israel were within God's governance.

views.label: Calamity as a moral consequence under the covenant
views.case: The blessings and curses of Deuteronomy 28 tied national disaster to national disobedience, and Amos 4:6-11 lists the very disasters named there. So the calamity of verse 6 is read in the covenant frame as the judgment God had said would come, not as a general statement that God is the author of every evil.

views.label: A claim about sovereignty, not about moral evil
views.case: The word ra'ah can mean calamity or harm, and does not necessarily mean moral evil. Many readers distinguish between God ordering disaster as part of His just governance and God doing wrong. James 1:13 insists that God cannot be tempted by evil and does not tempt anyone.

debates.bearing: All three agree that Amos is claiming that nothing outside God's rule has overtaken the cities. They differ on how widely to apply it. The safe path is to apply it as Amos does, to the covenant people under the warnings they had been given, and to trust the wider teaching of Scripture that God is just and good in all His ways, Deuteronomy 32:4.

debates.question: What is the point of the shepherd's rescue in verse 12?

views.label: A grim remnant: only evidence of the loss
views.case: Exodus 22:13 allows a shepherd to produce the torn remains as proof that a beast took the animal. Two legs or a piece of an ear are not a rescue; they are evidence. On this reading the corner of a bed is all that remains of the rich man's house, and the verse is a picture of total destruction.

views.label: A glimmer of mercy
views.case: Others note that the verb 'rescued' is the language of deliverance and that Amos elsewhere speaks of a remnant, 5:15 and 9:8. On this reading even in the midst of judgment a handful will be saved, though they will be a small and shabby handful.

debates.bearing: The first reading fits the legal background and the sentence of the context. The second does not require the first to be false, since a remnant survives in the later chapters. But in this verse the emphasis falls on how little remains, and not on the one who rescues.

debates.question: Is the last line of verse 12 secure in the Hebrew?

views.label: The BSB reading
views.case: The Israelites in Samaria are rescued with 'just the corner of a bed or the cushion of a couch.' The Hebrew is difficult, and this takes it as describing the scraps of furniture that the wealthy will keep.

views.label: The alternative in the footnote
views.case: The BSB footnote records another reading, 'on the edge of their beds and in Damascus on their couches,' which takes one rare word as the name of the city of Damascus. On this reading the wealthy are pictured lounging at ease, then snatched away.

debates.bearing: The text is uncertain here, and honest readers say so. The main sense is unaffected: the luxury of Samaria's rich will not save them, and what is saved will be small.

study.originalLanguages:
Begin with the verb that bears most of the weight of the chapter, the one translated 'punish' in verse 2 and 'visit' in verse 14. It is paqad, a word with a wide range: to attend to, to muster, to appoint, to visit with care, and to visit with judgment. God 'visited' Sarah in Genesis 21:1 with a child, and He 'visits' the iniquity of the fathers in Exodus 34:7. In Amos 3:2 it is the verb of the Judge, and the 'therefore' that opens the clause in the Hebrew is what shocks. The chosen are 'visited' because they are known.

The 'known' of verse 2 is yada, which the footnote notes can be rendered 'chosen,' but Genesis 18:19 gives a useful comparison. The LORD says of Abraham, 'I have chosen him,' where the word is again yada, and the purpose clause that follows is that Abraham will teach his household 'to keep the way of the LORD by doing what is right and just.' To be known is to be called to something. Amos is reading the election of Israel in its original sense, as a summons with a purpose, and he asks what became of the purpose.

Verse 3 asks whether two can walk together unless they have agreed. The verb is ya'ad, whose basic sense is to meet by appointment, and it shares its root with the noun for an appointed time, mo'ed, which is the word used for the festivals. The footnote says, 'Or without an appointment to meet.' If that is the sense, the question asks whether two people can find themselves walking together by chance, and the implied answer is that God and Israel's coincidence on the same road cannot be an accident. Either way the force is the same: shared direction has to be explained, and so does a warning.

Verse 7 says that God reveals His 'plan,' sod, to the prophets. The word means a circle of intimates, a council, and then the confidential counsel that is shared within it. In Jeremiah 23:18 the true prophet is the one who has 'stood in the council of the LORD.' Psalm 25:14 uses it for the friendship of the LORD, which is for those who fear Him. In Amos the prophet is not a seer who has special powers but a trusted confidant of the heavenly king, and that is what gives his word force.

In verse 10, the people 'know not how to do right.' The word is nekochah, which carries the sense of what is straightforward or right before one's eyes. The people have lost the ability to do what is plainly right. What they 'store up' in their citadels is chamas and shod, violence and destruction, a pair of words that elsewhere stand for the wreck of a society. They are accumulating in their strongholds the very thing they will be paid in.

The altar 'horns' of verse 14, qarnot, are the same word for the horns of animals. Cutting them off is a legal act as well as a physical one. It closes the last asylum. And the 'great houses,' batim rabbim, at the end of verse 15, gather the sentence in a phrase: the ivory, the winter house and the summer house will all come to an end.

typology.type: The prophet in the council of the LORD, Amos 3:7
typology.fulfillment: Amos claims access to God's confidential plan, and Jeremiah 23:18 makes standing in that council the mark of a true prophet. Jesus is the one who actually comes from the council. 'No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known,' John 1:18, and He says, 'We speak of what we know,' John 3:11. The correspondence is of a messenger who relays what he has been given. The escalation is that Amos was told what the Lord was about to do, while Jesus is the Word who was with God. The type falls short because the prophet was a servant, and the Son is a friend who tells His followers everything, John 15:15.

typology.type: The horns of the altar cut off, Amos 3:14
typology.fulfillment: The altar at Bethel was a place of apparent refuge, and its horns, which a fugitive might grasp, will be cut off. It is a picture of the failure of every false shelter. The New Testament speaks of a true altar and a true refuge. Hebrews 13:10 says that 'we have an altar,' and Hebrews 6:18 speaks of those who 'have fled to take hold of the hope set before us.' The escalation is that the place of safety is now a person, who was Himself sacrificed. The type falls short because the horns could be held by anyone with a claim, whereas the refuge in Christ is offered by faith and cannot be cut off.

typology.type: The shepherd who recovers scraps from the lion's mouth, Amos 3:12
typology.fulfillment: The shepherd of Amos can bring back only two legs or a piece of an ear. Jesus is the Good Shepherd, John 10:11, and He says of His sheep, 'No one can snatch them out of My hand,' John 10:28. The contrast is that where the earthly shepherd recovers only evidence, the Good Shepherd loses none of those the Father has given Him, John 6:39. The correspondence is of the shepherd, the predator and the flock, and the escalation is that the shepherd does not walk away from the encounter with fragments, but lays down His life and takes it up again. This is a pattern by contrast, and Amos did not intend it as a prediction.

typology.type: The chosen people held to account, Amos 3:2
typology.fulfillment: Israel is God's son, called out of Egypt, Hosea 11:1, and Matthew sees that calling renewed in the infant Jesus, who is carried to Egypt and brought back, Matthew 2:15. Where the nation, who was known above all the families of the earth, failed, Jesus is the true Israel who passes through the water and the wilderness and obeys, Matthew 3:13 to 4:11. The correspondence is of a chosen son. The escalation is that His obedience is credited to those who belong to Him. The type falls short in that the nation's calling was real but not enough, while Christ's faithfulness is a fully adequate answer to the standard of verse 2.

study.christ:
Amos 3 does not mention a coming deliverer, so the links to Christ must be drawn carefully from what the chapter does say. They concern the word, the refuge and the standard of judgment.

The first link is to Christ as the one who has the word from God. Amos claims, 'Surely the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets,' 3:7, and says that when God speaks the prophet cannot help but speak. Hebrews opens by saying that the God who spoke through the prophets 'on many past occasions and in many different ways' has 'in these last days' spoken to us by His Son, Hebrews 1:1-2. The line from verse 7 to the Son is a line from servants to the one who is Himself the Word. John says that He was with God in the beginning and was God, and that no one has ever seen God but the Son has made Him known, John 1:1 and John 1:18. What Amos had by commission, Jesus has by nature. Jesus also says that He does what He sees the Father doing and that the Father shows Him everything, John 5:19-20. He is the prophet who needs no council, since He is of the council.

The second link is to Christ as the answer to the failing refuge. The horns of the altar at Bethel offered a last claim to mercy, and Amos says they will fall to the ground. A refuge that God's own judgment removes can be no refuge. The New Testament says that the sacrifices of the old altar could never take away sins, Hebrews 10:4, and presents Christ as the one sacrifice for sins for all time, Hebrews 10:12. He is also the one into whose hands the fugitive may run. Hebrews 6:18 says that we have 'fled to take hold of the hope set before us,' and the wording echoes the language of the altar and the fugitive. The false altar is cut down so that the true one is seen.

The third link is Christ as the one on whom the standard of verse 2 falls. 'Only you have I known,' says God, and the consequence is the visit of a judge. Israel was supposed to be the child who was faithful to the Father. Where Israel failed, Jesus is the Son who was called out of Egypt, Matthew 2:15, and passed through the waters and was tested in the wilderness for forty days, and did not fall. His faithfulness is counted for those who believe, Romans 5:19. The one who is known most closely by the Father is the one who has drunk the cup of judgment for those who are known less faithfully.

A fourth and quieter link is to the shepherd. The shepherd in verse 12 is a figure of recovering only fragments, and the Good Shepherd is a figure of losing none, John 6:39. The comparison is not a prophecy, but the contrast clarifies what Christ's rescue is. The remnant that survives under Amos is a few pieces of furniture. The remnant that survives under Christ is every one of those given to Him, whole, and raised on the last day.

The reader should be careful not to press every detail into a picture of Jesus. The lion, the trap and the trumpet are arguments about cause and effect and are not coded. What the chapter gives is the pattern of word, refuge and judgment that Christ fulfils.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who has a particular relationship and takes it seriously. 'Only you have I known' is the language of intimacy, and the God who speaks it does not treat intimacy as indifference. The Bible's pictures of His love for His people, a husband for a wife in Hosea 2, a father for a son in Hosea 11, are matched by the seriousness of Amos. The God who loves is also the God who judges the beloved, and the two are not in tension. Those who are closest to Him are those from whom He asks the most, and love that never corrects is not love.

He is the God who speaks before He acts. Verse 7 says that He does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets. This is a statement about the character of God's rule. He does not manage history in secret and spring judgment on a surprised people. Between the decision and the event there is a warning, and Israel's trouble is that the warning has been given and they have paid no attention. The same pattern appears in Genesis 18, where He tells Abraham of Sodom's fate, and in Jonah, where Nineveh is told of coming judgment forty days ahead. A God who warns is a God who hopes that the warning will be heeded.

He is sovereign over calamity as well as blessing. The sixth question puts the matter bluntly: if disaster comes to a city, has the LORD not done it? The doctrine of God here is hard, and the Bible does not dodge it, Isaiah 45:7 and Lamentations 3:37-38. It does not, however, make Him arbitrary. The calamity of Amos is tied to specific warnings, the word of the covenant and the charges of 2:6-8 and 3:10. This is a sovereignty that is moral through and through. The reader should hold alongside it the testimony of Deuteronomy 32:4, that He is a God of faithfulness without injustice, and James 1:13, that He tempts no one.

He is the God who calls witnesses and conducts a fair trial. Ashdod and Egypt are not asked to condemn; they are asked to observe, and to judge whether what they see in Samaria is a society that knows how to do right. The God who invites such scrutiny is one who has nothing to hide in the process. He is also a God whose standard cannot be argued down by comparison: what Israel does is judged against the exodus and the law and not against what the neighbours do.

He is the God who cuts away false refuge. The altar, the ivory houses and the summer and winter homes are the structures in which people felt secure, and He deals with each. The mercy hidden in this is that He will not allow His people to settle on something that cannot hold. For worship, the chapter asks us to be grateful for being known and to answer that knowledge with the attention it deserves, and to pray as the psalm does, 'Search me, O God, and know my heart,' Psalm 139:23.

crossReferences.note: The LORD asks, 'Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?' and gives as the reason that He has chosen him so that he will teach his household to keep the way of the LORD and do what is right and just. It is the best commentary on Amos 3:2 and 3:7, since it joins knowing, revealing and the duty to justice.

Moses explains that Israel was chosen not because it was numerous but because the LORD loved them and kept His oath. The same election that Moses presents as the ground of gratitude is turned by Amos into the ground of accountability, and the two belong together.

The LORD complains of prophets who have not stood in His council, and says that if they had, they would have proclaimed His words and turned the people from their evil. It supplies the background for the 'plan' of Amos 3:7 and measures the claim of every would-be prophet.

Jeremiah says that if he tries to stop speaking in God's name, His word becomes a fire shut up in his bones and he cannot hold it in. It is the personal experience behind Amos 3:8, where the prophet says that he cannot keep silent once the LORD has spoken.

The law lays out what a shepherd owes if an animal in his care dies. If it was torn by a beast, he brings the remains as evidence and need not make restitution. This is the background for the shepherd of Amos 3:12 and shows that what he brings back is proof of loss rather than a rescue.

Adonijah fled to the altar and took hold of its horns, and Solomon granted him a conditional pardon. The scene shows the horns as a place of refuge for the desperate, which is the reason their removal in Amos 3:14 is so alarming.

Micah summons the mountains and hills to hear the LORD's case against His people. The summoning of witnesses in the court of the world matches the call to the strongholds of Ashdod and Egypt to assemble on the mountains of Samaria and observe.

Jesus teaches that those who knew the master's will and did not do it will be beaten with many blows, and that from everyone given much, much will be required. This is the plainest New Testament statement of the principle of Amos 3:2.

The mystery of God will be fulfilled 'just as He proclaimed to His servants the prophets.' The language is very close to Amos 3:7 and shows that the final book of the Bible treats that verse as true to the end, with the plan of God revealed to the prophets before it comes to pass.

The God who spoke to the fathers through the prophets has in these last days spoken by His Son. This takes the line of Amos 3:7 to its end: the prophets were the earlier servants who received God's word, and the Son is the one through whom He has spoken most fully.

study.oneStory:
The chapter belongs to the part of the Bible's story in which God has chosen a people and set them among the nations as a light, and the people have begun to wear that calling as a badge. Back in Genesis 12:1-3 Abraham is called to be a blessing, and Exodus 19:4-6 says that Israel will be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. Amos 3:2 does not reverse those promises. It insists on what they always carried, that a people near to God must show His character to the world.

The question that Amos raises is the one the rest of the Old Testament tries to answer: what happens when the chosen people fail the purpose of their choosing? The prophets show that the failure is not a single moment but a long decline. Amos describes it in the eighth century, Isaiah and Micah after him, and Jeremiah and Ezekiel at the end. The altars of Bethel fall in the end, and Samaria falls to Assyria in 722 BC, 2 Kings 17:5-6. Judah falls to Babylon, and the temple itself is burned, 2 Kings 25:8-9.

Even so, the same chapter that threatens carries a promise in its structure. Because God reveals His plans to the prophets before He acts, there is always time to turn. And the shepherd's remnant, however small, is a sign that God does not abandon everything. Amos 9:8 says that He will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob, and Amos 9:11-15 promises the restoration of David's fallen tent. The pattern that the whole Old Testament follows is that judgment is never the last word God speaks to the people He has known.

The answer comes in Jesus. The true Israel is the Son who was called out of Egypt, Matthew 2:15, and who is the one in whom the knowledge of verse 2 is fulfilled. Where Israel carried the privilege and the failure, He carries the privilege and the obedience, and then takes up the failure in His death. The people who belong to Him are called a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, 1 Peter 2:9, and the language of Exodus 19 is turned into the description of the church. And they are warned in the same passage that judgment begins with God's household, 1 Peter 4:17. The standard of Amos 3:2 has not been lowered.

The story ends where the roar of Amos began, in the presence of the one who is known and who knows. In the new creation, God's servants 'will see His face,' Revelation 22:4. The knowledge of 'Only you have I known' is completed in the knowledge in which His people see Him, and the altars of false refuge are replaced by a city whose temple is the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb, Revelation 21:22.

quiz.q: What does God mean by only you have I known, therefore I will punish you?

options.text: Israel's unique covenant intimacy with God raises their accountability rather than exempting them.
options.note: Being chosen means greater responsibility, not immunity.

options.text: God knows everything about everyone, so no sin is hidden.
options.note: The word here is covenant choosing, not general omniscience.

options.text: God had a special relationship with Israel that made their rebellion worse.
options.note: Right about the special relationship; the sharp point is that it increases accountability.

options.text: God had abandoned Israel and no longer knew them.
options.note: The opposite: it is precisely because He knew them that He acts.

quiz.q: Why does Amos pile up questions about lions, traps, and trumpets?

options.text: To show that effects have causes, so his prophesying is the unavoidable echo of God having spoken.
options.note: The lion has roared, so the prophet must speak; nothing is random.

options.text: To display his knowledge of nature as a shepherd.
options.note: The images serve an argument, not a nature lesson.

options.text: To argue that disasters and warnings always have a reason behind them.
options.note: True, and the climax is that God's word compels the prophet to speak.

options.text: To entertain the crowd with riddles.
options.note: These are pointed arguments, not entertainment.

quiz.q: Why does God summon Ashdod and Egypt to look at Samaria?

options.text: Even pagan nations can see Israel's oppression is appalling, witnessing against God's own people.
options.note: The enemies become witnesses to Israel's injustice.

options.text: God wanted to form an alliance with them.
options.note: They are summoned as witnesses to judgment, not allies.

options.text: To shame Israel by comparison with outsiders.
options.note: Right about the shame; specifically they testify to the oppression in Samaria.

options.text: Because they were more righteous than Israel.
options.note: They are called as witnesses, not held up as righteous.

quiz.q: What is the significance of cutting off the horns of the altar at Bethel?

options.text: It declares that Israel's false worship offers no refuge or atonement, pointing to the need for the true altar in Christ.
options.note: The horns were the place of asylum and atonement; their fall ends counterfeit worship.

options.text: It was simply property damage to a building.
options.note: The horns carried deep religious meaning; this is judgment on false worship.

options.text: It ended the sanctuary that had been a place of asylum and sacrifice.
options.note: Correct about asylum and sacrifice; the deeper point is the futility of false worship and the need for Christ.

options.text: It restored proper worship at Bethel.
options.note: It destroys Bethel's worship rather than restoring it.

quiz.q: What does Amos 3:7 teach about how God works?

options.text: God does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets; He warns before He acts.
options.note: God speaks before He acts, in mercy and justice.

options.text: God keeps all His plans completely secret.
options.note: The verse says the opposite: He reveals His plans to the prophets.

options.text: God communicates His purposes through chosen messengers.
options.note: Right, and specifically He does nothing in judgment without first warning through them.

options.text: God only acts after human beings figure out His will.
options.note: God initiates and reveals; He does not wait on human discovery.

questions: God says being chosen made Israel more accountable, not less. Where are you tempted to treat God's grace to you as a license rather than a responsibility?
Amos could not keep silent once God had spoken. Is there truth God has made clear to you that you are avoiding speaking or obeying?
Even pagan nations could see the oppression in Samaria. What might outsiders honestly observe about the way you or your community treat the vulnerable?
The luxurious houses and false altars were both torn down. What comforts or forms of religion are you leaning on that cannot finally hold?
God always warns before He acts. How does His patience in speaking before judging move you to listen to Him today?

translationNotes.note: Known translates yada, which carries the sense of covenant choosing and intimate relationship, not mere awareness; a footnote tradition renders it chosen.
The two clauses are parallel rhetorical questions.
The image of a shepherd salvaging two legs or an ear from a lion's mouth pictures a rescue so minimal it is really a proof of death; only scraps of Samaria's luxury will remain.
